# Contributing to React

Want to contribute to React? There are a few things you need to know.  

We wrote a **[contribution guide](https://reactjs.org/docs/how-to-contribute.html)** to help you get started.

# [React](https://react.dev/) · [![GitHub license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/LICENSE) [![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/react.svg?style=flat)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/react) [![(Runtime) Build and Test](https://github.com/facebook/react/actions/workflows/runtime_build_and_test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/facebook/react/actions/workflows/runtime_build_and_test.yml) [![(Compiler) TypeScript](https://github.com/facebook/react/actions/workflows/compiler_typescript.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/facebook/react/actions/workflows/compiler_typescript.yml) [![PRs Welcome](https://img.shields.io/badge/PRs-welcome-brightgreen.svg)](https://legacy.reactjs.org/docs/how-to-contribute.html#your-first-pull-request) React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. * **Declarative:** React makes it painless to create interactive UIs. Design simple views for each state in your application, and React will efficiently update and render just the right components when your data changes. Declarative views make your code more predictable, simpler to understand, and easier to debug. * **Component-Based:** Build encapsulated components that manage their own state, then compose them to make complex UIs. Since component logic is written in JavaScript instead of templates, you can easily pass rich data through your app and keep the state out of the DOM. * **Learn Once, Write Anywhere:** We don't make assumptions about the rest of your technology stack, so you can develop new features in React without rewriting existing code. React can also render on the server using [Node](https://nodejs.org/en) and power mobile apps using [React Native](https://reactnative.dev/). [Learn how to use React in your project](https://react.dev/learn). ## Installation React has been designed for gradual adoption from the start, and **you can use as little or as much React as you need**: * Use [Quick Start](https://react.dev/learn) to get a taste of React. * [Add React to an Existing Project](https://react.dev/learn/add-react-to-an-existing-project) to use as little or as much React as you need. * [Create a New React App](https://react.dev/learn/start-a-new-react-project) if you're looking for a powerful JavaScript toolchain. ## Documentation You can find the React documentation [on the website](https://react.dev/). Check out the [Getting Started](https://react.dev/learn) page for a quick overview. The documentation is divided into several sections: * [Quick Start](https://react.dev/learn) * [Tutorial](https://react.dev/learn/tutorial-tic-tac-toe) * [Thinking in React](https://react.dev/learn/thinking-in-react) * [Installation](https://react.dev/learn/installation) * [Describing the UI](https://react.dev/learn/describing-the-ui) * [Adding Interactivity](https://react.dev/learn/adding-interactivity) * [Managing State](https://react.dev/learn/managing-state) * [Advanced Guides](https://react.dev/learn/escape-hatches) * [API Reference](https://react.dev/reference/react) * [Where to Get Support](https://react.dev/community) * [Contributing Guide](https://legacy.reactjs.org/docs/how-to-contribute.html) You can improve it by sending pull requests to [this repository](https://github.com/reactjs/react.dev). ## Examples We have several examples [on the website](https://react.dev/). Here is the first one to get you started: ```jsx import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'; function HelloMessage({ name }) { return
Hello {name}
; } const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('container')); root.render(); ``` This example will render "Hello Taylor" into a container on the page. You'll notice that we used an HTML-like syntax; [we call it JSX](https://react.dev/learn#writing-markup-with-jsx). JSX is not required to use React, but it makes code more readable, and writing it feels like writing HTML. ## Contributing The main purpose of this repository is to continue evolving React core, making it faster and easier to use. Development of React happens in the open on GitHub, and we are grateful to the community for contributing bugfixes and improvements. Read below to learn how you can take part in improving React. ### [Code of Conduct](https://code.fb.com/codeofconduct) Facebook has adopted a Code of Conduct that we expect project participants to adhere to. Please read [the full text](https://code.fb.com/codeofconduct) so that you can understand what actions will and will not be tolerated. ### [Contributing Guide](https://legacy.reactjs.org/docs/how-to-contribute.html) Read our [contributing guide](https://legacy.reactjs.org/docs/how-to-contribute.html) to learn about our development process, how to propose bugfixes and improvements, and how to build and test your changes to React. ### [Good First Issues](https://github.com/facebook/react/labels/good%20first%20issue) To help you get your feet wet and get you familiar with our contribution process, we have a list of [good first issues](https://github.com/facebook/react/labels/good%20first%20issue) that contain bugs that have a relatively limited scope. report.overview: This is the facebook/react monorepo at commit 59aff3e — the React runtime (isomorphic `react`, the Fiber reconciler, the Fizz SSR server, the Flight/Server-Components client+server, DevTools, and the Scheduler) plus a largely independent `compiler/` sub-project holding the React Compiler in both TypeScript (`babel-plugin-react-compiler`) and an in-progress Rust port (12 `react_compiler_*` crates behind a napi bridge). It is a library-publishing repo, not an app: nearly every artifact is a Rollup-built npm bundle produced per *release channel* (stable / canary / experimental / www-classic / www-modern / xplat), with behaviour toggled by ~67 `enable*` feature flags that are fork-substituted at build time. What is distinctive is the fork/shim architecture — `ReactFiberConfig`, `ReactFeatureFlags`, `ReactFlightServerConfig` and friends are placeholder modules that *throw* unless Rollup or Jest swaps in a renderer-specific implementation — and a CI matrix that runs the same Jest suite 18 ways × 5 shards to prove every channel behaves.

system_map.summary: There is no single entrypoint; the repo is a set of publishable packages under `packages/` (workspace glob in `package.json`) plus a nested Yarn/Cargo workspace under `compiler/`. The public runtime entrypoints are `packages/react/index.js` (isomorphic), `packages/react-dom/client.js` → `ReactDOMRoot.createRoot`, `packages/react-dom/server.node.js` → Fizz, and `packages/react-server-dom-*/server.*` → Flight. Everything is compiled by `scripts/rollup/build.js`, driven by a bundle table in `scripts/rollup/bundles.js` and a module-substitution table in `scripts/rollup/forks.js`; `build-all-release-channels.js` runs the whole thing once per channel and rewrites versions from `ReactVersions.js`. There is no database or persistent storage layer — the only 'storage' is the Fiber tree in memory, npm as the deployment target, and GitHub Actions artifacts. Tests never run `jest` directly; `scripts/jest/jest-cli.js` picks one of six configs and spawns Jest with channel/env/variant globals injected.

claims.claim: `package.json` declares a Yarn-1 workspace over `packages/*` with `packageManager: yarn@1.22.22`, and blocks direct Jest invocation via `"jest": {"testRegex": "/scripts/jest/dont-run-jest-directly\\.js$"}` — all testing must go through `yarn test` → `scripts/jest/jest-cli.js`.

`ReactVersions.js` is the single source of truth for publishing: `ReactVersion = '19.3.0'`, a `stablePackages` map (react-reconciler 0.34.0, scheduler 0.28.0, react-refresh 0.19.0, eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1) and `experimentalPackages = ['react-markup']`; a package not listed there is never published.

The client entrypoint is `createRoot(container, options)` in `packages/react-dom/src/client/ReactDOMRoot.js`, which calls `createContainer(..., ConcurrentRoot, ...)`, `markContainerAsRoot`, then `listenToAllSupportedEvents(rootContainerElement)` before returning a `ReactDOMRoot` wrapper whose `.render` delegates to `updateContainer`.

The reconciler's public surface is `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberReconciler.js` — `createContainer`, `updateContainer`, `updateContainerSync`, and `updateContainerImpl` which builds an update via `createUpdate(lane)` / `enqueueUpdate` and hands off to `scheduleUpdateOnFiber(root, rootFiber, lane)`.

The renderer boundary is the `ReactFiberConfig` shim: `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberConfig.js` contains only `throw new Error('This module must be shimmed by a specific renderer.')` — Rollup (`scripts/rollup/forks.js`) and Jest (`scripts/jest/setupHostConfigs.js`) both substitute a real host config per renderer.

`scripts/shared/inlinedHostConfigs.js` enumerates ~20 renderer targets by `shortName` (`dom-browser`, `dom-node`, `dom-edge-webpack`, `dom-node-turbopack`, `dom-node-parcel`, `dom-bun`, `fabric`, `markup`, `dom-fb`, …), each with an `entryPoints` list — this table is the authoritative list of runtime boundaries.

Cooperative scheduling lives in `packages/scheduler/src/forks/Scheduler.js`: `unstable_scheduleCallback` pushes into a min-heap, `workLoop` drains it, and `shouldYieldToHost` yields once `timeElapsed >= frameInterval` (default `frameYieldMs`, tunable via an fps setter); the host callback is scheduled via `setImmediate` when available, else `MessageChannel` (chosen to dodge the 4 ms `setTimeout` clamp), else `setTimeout`.

Builds are orchestrated by `scripts/rollup/build.js` (`buildEverything` → `createBundle` per bundle × bundleType, with Babel, Google Closure Compiler for prod bundles, and `rollup-plugin-prettier` for FB/dev output) over the ~20 `bundleTypes` declared in `scripts/rollup/bundles.js` (NODE_DEV/PROD/PROFILING, ESM_*, BUN_*, FB_WWW_*, RN_OSS_*, RN_FB_*, BROWSER_SCRIPT, CJS_DTS/ESM_DTS).

`scripts/rollup/build-all-release-channels.js` shells out to the build once per channel via `spawnSync`, then `processStable(buildDir)` / `processExperimental(buildDir)` rewrite package versions using the short SHA from `git rev-parse HEAD`, merging the experimental tree into the stable one.

The compiler is a second workspace: `compiler/Cargo.toml` defines a Rust workspace over `crates/*` plus `packages/babel-plugin-react-compiler-rust/native`, pinned to edition 2024 / rust-version 1.85, version `0.0.1-oidc.0`, with a `[profile.release]` of fat LTO + 1 codegen unit + strip (documented as shrinking the shipped `index.node` from 11.2 MB to 7.2 MB).

The Rust compiler is reached from JS through napi: `native/src/lib.rs` exposes `#[napi] pub fn compile(ast_json, scope_json, options_json) -> String`, spawning a dedicated 64 MB-stack thread and catching panics; `src/bridge.ts` loads it with `require('../native')` and passes JSON.

External integrations are narrow and mostly tooling-side: npm registry (`scripts/release/publish.js`, `scripts/release/ci-npmrc`), Discord webhooks in four notify workflows, Vercel for the compiler playground (`compiler/apps/playground/vercel.json`), and Algolia's `beta-react` index queried by the React MCP server.

Deployment shape is 'publish to npm from CI': `compiler_prereleases.yml`, `compiler_prereleases_nightly.yml` and `compiler_prereleases_manual.yml` inject `NPM_TOKEN` into the job env, while `scripts/release/publish.js` notes that npm `whoami`/ownership checks were removed in favour of OIDC trusted publishing.

Repo-level agent conventions are codified in `CLAUDE.md` plus `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` — `/verify` runs `yarn prettier` → `yarn linc` → `/flow` + `/test` + `/test www` in parallel, and explicitly instructs that builds are CI's job and should not be run locally.

feature_catalog.summary: User-facing surface is API surface, not screens. `packages/react/src/ReactClient.js` is the canonical export list for the isomorphic package; `react-dom` fans out to client, server (Node/Edge/Browser/Bun), static prerender and test-utils entrypoints; `react-server-dom-{webpack,turbopack,parcel,esm,unbundled,fb}` each ship a bundler-specific Flight client+server pair. Tooling packages are first-class features too: `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` (now also re-exporting compiler-derived rules), `react-refresh` (Fast Refresh Babel plugin + runtime), DevTools in five packaging flavours, and two MCP servers. Behaviour is further gated by ~67 `enable*` flags in `packages/shared/ReactFeatureFlags.js`, inspectable via `yarn flags`.

claims.claim: The isomorphic `react` package exports the full modern surface including `use`, `cache`, `cacheSignal`, `Activity`, `ViewTransition`, `addTransitionType`, `unstable_SuspenseList`, `unstable_TracingMarker`, and `__COMPILER_RUNTIME` — enumerated in `packages/react/index.js` and implemented in `ReactClient.js`.

Hooks are exported from `packages/react/src/ReactHooks.js` and include the newer `useOptimistic`, `useActionState`, `useEffectEvent`, `useSyncExternalStore`, `useDeferredValue`, `useCacheRefresh` and `use`.

`react-dom` ships eleven distinct entrypoints — `client.js`, `server.js`/`server.node.js`/`server.edge.js`/`server.browser.js`/`server.bun.js`, `static.js`/`static.node.js`/`static.edge.js`/`static.browser.js`, `profiling.js`, `test-utils.js`, `unstable_testing.js` and `unstable_server-external-runtime.js`.

Streaming SSR is `renderToPipeableStream` in `packages/react-dom/src/server/ReactDOMFizzServerNode.js`, which builds a request via `createRequestImpl` → `createRequest`, kicks off `startWork(request)`, and exposes `pipe(destination)` that calls `startFlowing(request, destination)`.

Server Actions are a shipped feature: `decodeAction(body, serverManifest)` scans FormData for `$ACTION_REF_*` / `$ACTION_ID_*` keys, resolves the reference through `loadServerReference`, and returns the action pre-bound to the remaining FormData; `decodeFormState` handles `$ACTION_KEY` for `useActionState`.

Flight (RSC) supports multiple request body shapes on the server: `decodeReply`, `decodeReplyFromBusboy` (multipart uploads) and `decodeReplyFromAsyncIterable`, all exported from `ReactFlightDOMServerNode.js`.

Taint APIs `taintUniqueValue` and `taintObjectReference` guard against leaking server secrets to the client, backed by `TaintRegistryObjects` (WeakMap), `TaintRegistryValues` (refcounted Map) and a `FinalizationRegistry` cleanup hook; gated by `enableTaint = __EXPERIMENTAL__`.

`eslint-plugin-react-hooks` v7 ships `rules-of-hooks` and `exhaustive-deps` plus a set of compiler-derived rules merged in from `shared/ReactCompiler`, with `recommended` and `recommendedLatest` flat-config presets and a deprecated-rule shim for `component-hook-factories`.
Fast Refresh is two artifacts: `ReactFreshBabelPlugin.js` (build-time instrumentation) and `ReactFreshRuntime.js` (runtime registry / signature checking), published as `react-refresh@0.19.0`.

DevTools ships in five packaging flavours — `react-devtools` (standalone), `-core`, `-extensions` (browser extension), `-inline`, `-fusebox` (React Native / Chrome DevTools frontend) — all sharing `react-devtools-shared`, plus `react-devtools-shell` for local development.
`react-devtools-cdt-mcp` is a browser library that registers React inspection and profiling tools with `chrome-devtools-mcp`, published from its own workflow.

A second MCP server lives in the compiler: `compiler/packages/react-mcp-server` registers tools including `query-react-dev-docs` (Algolia-backed react.dev search) and a runtime-performance tool driven by headless Puppeteer.
The compiler playground is a real deployed Next.js 15.5.9 + Tailwind + Monaco app with a `dev` script that concurrently watches the compiler, the runtime and Next, and a Playwright `test` script.

CLI-style developer commands are exposed as npm scripts: `yarn test` (channel-aware), `yarn flow`, `yarn lint`/`yarn linc`, `yarn flags`, `yarn extract-errors`, `yarn download-build`, `yarn generate-changelog`, `yarn build-for-devtools`.

Behaviour is switchable at build time through ~67 `enable*` constants in `packages/shared/ReactFeatureFlags.js` (e.g. `enableViewTransition`, `enableGestureTransition`, `enableDefaultTransitionIndicator`, `enableFizzBlockingRender`, `enableOptimisticKey`), many tied to `__EXPERIMENTAL__`.

data_flow.summary: On the client, input enters through DOM events (delegated at the root by `listenToAllSupportedEvents`) or imperative `root.render`, both of which funnel into `scheduleUpdateOnFiber(root, fiber, lane)`. State lives on the Fiber tree hanging off `FiberRoot`; the `lane` bitmask on `ReactFiberLane.js` is the priority currency that decides whether work is flushed synchronously, in a microtask, or via a Scheduler task. Output boundaries are the host config (`ReactFiberConfig`, substituted per renderer) and, for SSR/RSC, the stream `Destination` in Fizz/Flight. Cross-module state is deliberately routed through a single mutable singleton, `ReactSharedInternals` (`.H` = current hooks dispatcher, `.T` = current transition, `.A` = async dispatcher), which is itself a forked module so client and server get different instances.

claims.claim: All client updates converge on `scheduleUpdateOnFiber`, which marks the root (`markRootUpdated(root, lane)`), merges interleaved/render-phase lanes, and calls `ensureRootIsScheduled(root)`; sync updates on legacy roots additionally trigger `flushSyncWorkOnLegacyRootsOnly()` immediately.

`ensureRootIsScheduled` does not schedule work directly — it appends the root to an intrusive linked list (`firstScheduledRoot`/`lastScheduledRoot` via `root.next`), sets `mightHavePendingSyncWork = true`, and defers to a microtask that runs `processRootScheduleInMicrotask` → `scheduleTaskForRootDuringMicrotask`.

Priority is encoded as a 31-bit lane bitmask (`TotalLanes = 31`) with named lanes `SyncLane`, `InputContinuousLane`, `DefaultLane`, transition lanes, retry lanes, `IdleLane`, `OffscreenLane` and `DeferredLane`; `requestUpdateLane(fiber)` picks the lane for each update.

`performWorkOnRoot` decides between `renderRootConcurrent` and `renderRootSync` from `shouldTimeSlice`, which is false for blocking lanes, expired lanes, or `forceSync` — but forced true when `checkIfRootIsPrerendering(root, lanes)` so prerendering never blocks the main thread.

External-store consistency is re-validated after a concurrent render: if `isRenderConsistentWithExternalStores(finishedWork)` fails, `performWorkOnRoot` discards the result and re-runs `renderRootSync(root, lanes, false)` to block further mutation.

Hook state is read and written through a swappable dispatcher on the shared-internals singleton: `renderWithHooks` assigns `ReactSharedInternals.H` to `HooksDispatcherOnMount` or `HooksDispatcherOnUpdate` (DEV variants included) and resets it to `ContextOnlyDispatcher` when the component finishes.

`root.render(children)` writes nothing directly — it calls `updateContainer(children, root, null, null)`, which becomes an update object on the host-root fiber's update queue via `createUpdate(lane)` + `enqueueUpdate(rootFiber, update, lane)`.

DOM events are the other input boundary and are delegated once per root: `createRoot` and `hydrateRoot` each call `listenToAllSupportedEvents(container)` from `react-dom-bindings/src/events/DOMPluginEventSystem`, so per-node listeners are not attached.

On the server, Fizz's data flow is request-scoped: `createRequest(...)` builds a `Request`, `startWork(request)` renders tasks (`retryTask`, `renderNode`, `renderNodeDestructive`), and `startFlowing(request, destination)` drains completed segments through `flushCompletedQueues` into the stream.

Server-Action input crosses a trust boundary as untyped `FormData`: `decodeAction` copies every non-`$ACTION_` field into a fresh `FormData`, decodes bound args by replaying them through `createResponse`/`getRoot` in `decodeBoundActionMetaData`, and binds the result — so client-supplied bytes drive `resolveServerReference(bundlerConfig, id)`.
`decodeBoundActionMetaData` accepts an `arraySizeLimit` parameter threaded into `createResponse`, indicating the Flight reply parser has an explicit bound on attacker-controlled array sizes.

DevTools data flows over a batched message bus: `Bridge` wraps a `Wall`, queues events and flushes them on a `BATCH_DURATION` timer, sending typed `BackendEvents` (`overrideProps`, `overrideHookState`, `overrideState`, `overrideContext`) from frontend to backend.

The renderer registers itself with the page-global `__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__` (installed by `installHook(target)` with `Object.defineProperty`, and explicitly documented as a de-facto public API) via `renderers.set(id, renderer)` — that global is the whole runtime↔DevTools data channel.

In the Rust compiler, data flows as JSON across the FFI boundary: Babel serialises the AST + scope info + options, `compile()` deserialises with `serde_json::Deserializer::disable_recursion_limit()` to survive deeply nested ASTs, and returns a JSON `CompileResult`.

The Rust HIR replaces JS shared-object references with arena indices: `identifiers`/`scopes`/`functions`/`types` vectors on `Environment`, addressed by `Copy` newtype IDs (`IdentifierId`, `ScopeId`, `FunctionId`, `TypeId`), with `HirFunction` deliberately not owning `env`.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows are worth walking: (1) client startup/first paint, from `createRoot` through the microtask scheduler into render and commit; (2) the compile flow, where Babel hands a function to either the TS `Pipeline.ts` or the Rust `pipeline.rs`; (3) the release flow, where a commit becomes npm artifacts. The commit phase in particular is a fixed three-pass sequence with `root.current = finishedWork` as the atomic swap point between mutation and layout, and passive effects flushed later. Each trace below names the functions in call order with line anchors.

claims.claim: Startup trace: `createRoot(container, options)` → validate via `isValidContainer` → `createContainer(container, ConcurrentRoot, …, onUncaughtError, onCaughtError, onRecoverableError)` → `markContainerAsRoot(root.current, container)` → `listenToAllSupportedEvents(rootContainerElement)` → `new ReactDOMRoot(root)`.

First render trace: `root.render(children)` → `updateContainer` → `updateContainerImpl` → `requestUpdateLane(current)` → `createUpdate(lane)` → `enqueueUpdate(rootFiber, update, lane)` → `scheduleUpdateOnFiber(root, rootFiber, lane)`.

Scheduling trace: `scheduleUpdateOnFiber` → `markRootUpdated(root, lane)` → `ensureRootIsScheduled(root)` → `ensureScheduleIsScheduled()` → `scheduleImmediateRootScheduleTask()` → (microtask) `processRootScheduleInMicrotask` → `scheduleTaskForRootDuringMicrotask` → `Scheduler_scheduleCallback(priorityLevel, performWorkOnRootViaSchedulerTask)`.

Render trace: `performWorkOnRoot(root, lanes, forceSync)` computes `shouldTimeSlice`, dispatches to `renderRootConcurrent` (line 2779) or `renderRootSync` (line 2623), then loops on the `RootExitStatus` — handling `RootInProgress` (yield, `startYieldTimer`), store inconsistency (re-render sync), and `RootErrored` (`getLanesToRetrySynchronouslyOnError` → `recoverFromConcurrentError`).

Component render trace: for each function component the reconciler calls `renderWithHooks`, which installs the mount-or-update dispatcher on `ReactSharedInternals.H`, invokes the component, then restores `ContextOnlyDispatcher`; `bailoutHooks` is the memoized fast path.

Commit trace: `commitRoot` (line 3725) → `commitBeforeMutationEffects(root, finishedWork, lanes)` → `commitMutationEffects(root, finishedWork, lanes)` → `root.current = finishedWork` (the tree swap, line 4051) → `commitLayoutEffects(finishedWork, root, lanes)` → `flushSpawnedWork()`; passive effects run later via `flushPendingEffects` → `commitPassiveMountEffects`.

Yield trace: inside a Scheduler task, `workLoop(initialTime)` drains the min-heap and stops when `shouldYieldToHost()` returns true (elapsed ≥ `frameInterval`); the continuation is re-armed by `schedulePerformWorkUntilDeadline()` through `setImmediate`/`MessageChannel`/`setTimeout`.

SSR trace: `renderToPipeableStream(children, options)` → `createRequestImpl` → `createRequest(...)` → `startWork(request)` (line 6370) → tasks retried through `retryTask`/`renderNode` → consumer calls `pipe(destination)` → `startFlowing(request, destination)` (line 6464) → `flushCompletedQueues` (line 6175); `abort(request, reason)` is the cancellation path (line 6557).

Server Action trace: HTTP POST FormData → `decodeAction(body, serverManifest)` → detect `$ACTION_REF_*` or `$ACTION_ID_*` → `decodeBoundActionMetaData` (for bound args) → `loadServerReference` → `resolveServerReference(bundlerConfig, id)` → `preloadModule` → `requireModule` → `bindArgs(fn, args)` → returned action `fn.bind(null, formData)`.

TS compile trace: `compileFn` builds `Environment` from `findContextIdentifiers(func)`, then runs `lower(func, env)` → `PruneMaybeThrows` → `ValidateContextVariableLValues` → `MergeConsecutiveBlocks` → `SSA` → `EliminateRedundantPhi` → `ConstantPropagation` → `InferTypes` → `AnalyseFunctions` → `InferMutationAliasingEffects` → `DeadCodeElimination` → `InferMutationAliasingRanges` → `InferReactivePlaces` → `buildReactiveFunction` → `renameVariables`, logging each step through the `log(value)` callback.

Rust compile trace mirrors it: `compile_fn` → `react_compiler_lowering::lower` → `validate_context_variable_lvalues` → `validate_use_memo` → `enter_ssa` → `eliminate_redundant_phi` → `infer_types` → `analyse_functions` → `infer_mutation_aliasing_effects` → `infer_mutation_aliasing_ranges` → validations → `infer_reactive_places` → `infer_reactive_scope_variables` → scope alignment passes.

The compiler is fault-tolerant rather than fail-fast: passes call `env.recordError(diagnostic)`, validation passes are wrapped in `env.tryRecord(() => pass(hir))`, and errors are aggregated at the end via `env.hasErrors()` / `env.aggregateErrors()` — `CompilerError.invariant()` is the only category that always throws.

Rust bailout trace: `prefilter.ts` walks the Babel AST first and only forwards functions that are component/hook declarations or carry an opt-in directive, so the napi boundary is never crossed for ordinary functions.

Release trace: `yarn build` → `prebuild` links the compiler via `scripts/react-compiler/link-compiler.sh` → `build-all-release-channels.js` → `buildForChannel(channel)` spawns `scripts/rollup/build.js` → `processStable`/`processExperimental` rewrite versions from `ReactVersions.js` + short SHA → `scripts/release/publish.js` validates tags and publishes with OIDC.

Error-minification trace: prod bundles emit `/*! <expected-error-format>"…"</expected-error-format>` markers; `yarn extract-errors` greps the `build` dir with `execSync('git --no-pager grep …')`, assigns the next free numeric code, and appends to `scripts/error-codes/codes.json` (~66 KB of registered messages).

testing_signals.summary: Jest 30 is the runtime test framework, with 544 test files under `packages/**/__tests__`, and it is deliberately unusable directly — `package.json`'s `testRegex` points at `dont-run-jest-directly.js`, forcing everything through `scripts/jest/jest-cli.js`. That CLI selects one of six configs (source, source-www, source-xplat, source-persistent, build, build-devtools) and injects `__DEV__`, `__EXPERIMENTAL__` and `__VARIANT__` globals; individual tests opt in/out of behaviour with `// @gate <flag>` pragmas resolved by `scripts/jest/TestFlags.js`. The compiler uses a different harness entirely: `yarn snap` over ~1,543 fixture files with `.expect.md` snapshots, plus Playwright e2e for the playground and the flight fixture. CI runs the runtime suite as an 18-config × 5-shard matrix; the Rust port has its own workflow gating on `cargo check`, `cargo build`, two shell test scripts and `yarn snap --rust`.

claims.claim: Jest is pinned at `^30.4.1` (`jest`, `jest-cli`, `jest-environment-jsdom`, `babel-jest`) with `jest-silent-reporter` and `jest-snapshot-serializer-raw` for output control.
There are 544 test files under `packages/**/__tests__/**/*.js`, spread across the runtime, DevTools shared, scheduler and shared packages.

`scripts/jest/jest-cli.js` is the only supported entry: it exposes `--project {default,devtools}`, `--releaseChannel {experimental,stable,www-classic,www-modern,xplat}`, `--env`, `--prod`/`--dev`, `--variant`, `--build`, `--persistent`, `--ci`, `--reactVersion` and `--sourceMaps`, then spawns Jest with the matching config file.

Six Jest configs cover the test surfaces: `config.source.js`, `config.source-www.js`, `config.source-xplat.js`, `config.source-persistent.js`, `config.build.js` and `config.build-devtools.js` — so the same specs are exercised against source and against built bundles.

`scripts/jest/setupHostConfigs.js` rewires module resolution so each test file resolves `react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberConfig` to the right renderer's host config, iterating over `inlinedHostConfigs` — without it every reconciler test would hit the throwing shim.

`packages/internal-test-utils` supplies the shared test vocabulary — `internalAct.js`, `ReactInternalTestUtils.js`, `consoleMock.js`, `shouldIgnoreConsoleError.js`/`shouldIgnoreConsoleWarn.js`, and `simulateBrowserEventDispatch.js` — and is itself tested.

The runtime CI matrix in `runtime_build_and_test.yml` runs 18 parameter sets (stable/experimental/www-classic/www-modern/xplat × development/production × variant true/false, plus two persistent configs) crossed with 5 shards, i.e. 90 parallel `yarn test` jobs.
CI also gates on non-test checks as separate jobs: `flow` (sharded by discovered inline configs), `check_generated_fizz_runtime`, `flags`, and `test-linter` for `eslint-plugin-react-hooks`.
There is a dedicated fuzz workflow (`runtime_fuzz_tests.yml`) separate from the main suite, so fuzzing is not part of the per-PR signal.

The compiler's test corpus is fixture-driven: ~1,543 `.js` fixtures under `babel-plugin-react-compiler/src/__tests__/fixtures`, each paired with a `.expect.md`, run via `yarn snap` (`-p <pattern>`, `-d` debug, `-u` update) as documented in `compiler/CLAUDE.md`.

Fixture naming encodes expected failure modes: `error.todo-*.js` means an unsupported feature that correctly bails with a Todo error, `error.bug-*.js` means a known bug producing the wrong error — so some fixtures are assertions about known gaps, not passing behaviour.

The Rust port has its own CI gate: `compiler_rust.yml` runs `cargo check`, `cargo build`, `bash scripts/test-babel-ast.sh`, `bash scripts/test-rust-port.sh`, then builds `snap` and runs `yarn snap --rust` — i.e. the Rust implementation is validated against the same fixture snapshots as the TS one.

Only 14 TypeScript unit-test files exist across the whole `compiler/` tree, versus 1,543 fixtures — the compiler's coverage is almost entirely end-to-end snapshot, with very little unit-level testing of individual passes.

risk_map.summary: The genuinely security-sensitive surface is small but sharp: Flight's Server Actions turn attacker-controlled FormData into a module lookup and function invocation, the taint registry is the only guard against serialising server secrets to the client and it is experimental-only, and the DevTools extension bridges page-world `postMessage` to privileged `chrome.runtime` ports while also running string-`eval` payloads through `chrome.devtools.inspectedWindow.eval`. Operationally the biggest fragility is the fork/shim system — `ReactFiberConfig` and `ReactFeatureFlags` resolve differently under Rollup, Jest and Flow, so a change that passes locally can break a channel nobody ran. `ReactFiberWorkLoop.js` at 5,683 lines with ~60 exported functions and module-level mutable state is the highest blast-radius file in the repo, and the Rust port is a live second implementation of the compiler that must stay snapshot-identical to the TypeScript one.

claims.claim: `loadServerReference` resolves a client-supplied string id straight into `resolveServerReference(bundlerConfig, id)` → `preloadModule` → `requireModule`; the only validation is `typeof id !== 'string'` (which silently returns `null as any`), so the security boundary rests entirely on the bundler-generated `serverManifest`.

`decodeAction` distinguishes action fields purely by string prefix (`$ACTION_REF_`, `$ACTION_ID_`, `$ACTION_`) on attacker-controlled FormData keys, and a mismatch falls through to `throw new Error('Cannot handle action key. This is a bug in React.')` — a user-reachable throw framed as an internal invariant.

The taint protection against leaking secrets to the client is gated off by default outside experimental builds (`export const enableTaint = __EXPERIMENTAL__`), and `taintUniqueValue` early-returns when the flag is false — stable consumers get no taint enforcement.

`TaintRegistryValues` is a plain `Map<string|bigint, TaintEntry>` with manual refcounting in `cleanup()`, relying on `FinalizationRegistry`; the code explicitly notes that if `FinalizationRegistry` is absent it 'assume[s] that objects live forever' — a correctness cliff on older runtimes.

The DevTools extension executes code as strings in the inspected page: `evalScripts.js` defines a `.code` variant for each of `checkIfReactPresentInInspectedWindow`, `reload`, `viewElementSource`, `viewAttributeSource` and the selection bridges, intended for `chrome.devtools.inspectedWindow.eval()`.

The extension's content scripts relay untrusted page-world messages into privileged extension ports: `prepareInjection.js` listens on `window.addEventListener('message', ...)` and `proxy.js` forwards across `chrome.runtime.connect(...)` / `chrome.runtime.onMessage` and back out via `window.postMessage` — a classic content-script trust boundary.

The DevTools bridge lets the frontend write arbitrary values into a live app — `overrideProps`, `overrideState`, `overrideHookState`, `overrideContext` are first-class bridge events — so anything that can speak the bridge protocol can mutate application state.
`__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__` is installed as a page global and documented in-source as 'a de facto public API', giving any script on the page a handle on every mounted renderer.

`ReactFiberWorkLoop.js` is 5,683 lines with roughly 60 exports and heavy module-level mutable state (`workInProgressRoot`, `workInProgressSuspendedReason`, `workInProgressRootExitStatus`, `executionContext`), making it the single highest blast-radius file — almost every reconciler behaviour change lands here.

The fork system is fragile by design: `scripts/rollup/forks.js` substitutes 13 module paths (shared internals, feature flags, fiber config, stream/fizz/flight configs, `EventListener`, `useSyncExternalStore`) and Jest substitutes them differently — so a module can resolve three ways (Rollup, Jest, Flow) and only CI exercises all of them.

There are 13 `ReactFeatureFlags` forks (`www`, `www-dynamic`, `native-fb`, `native-oss`, `test-renderer`, `eslint-plugin.www`, `readonly`, …); a flag added to the base file without updating every fork is a known failure mode, which is exactly why CI has a dedicated `flags` job and a `/flags` skill.

`scripts/release/ci-npmrc` writes `//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}` and three compiler prerelease workflows inject `NPM_TOKEN` from repository secrets — any workflow change that widens trigger conditions on those files widens publish access.

The MCP server's runtime-perf tool launches a real browser (`puppeteer.launch()`) and runs `page.evaluate` on supplied component code — that is code execution on the developer's machine driven by MCP tool input.

An Algolia app id and search API key are hard-coded in `compiler/packages/react-mcp-server/src/utils/algolia.ts` (with a source comment pointing at react.dev's public config) — low severity since they are public search-only credentials, but they are real credentials living in the tree.

The Rust port is a duplicated implementation of a complex pipeline: `compiler/crates/react_compiler/src/entrypoint/pipeline.rs` re-implements the same ~40 passes as `Pipeline.ts`, and `react_compiler/src/lib.rs` re-exports crates 'for backwards compatibility' — divergence between the two is caught only by `yarn snap --rust` in CI.

The napi bridge converts Rust panics into `napi::Error` strings rather than structured diagnostics, and relies on a hand-tuned 64 MB thread stack to avoid overflow on deep ASTs — both are heuristic mitigations rather than guarantees.

Legacy code is still resident and flag-guarded rather than removed: `disableLegacyMode`, `LegacyRoot`, `flushSyncWorkOnLegacyRootsOnly`, `isAlreadyFailedLegacyErrorBoundary`, `enableLegacyFBSupport` and `enableLegacyCache` all remain live branches in the work loop and flag file.

extension_points.summary: The repo's main extension mechanism is the host-config pattern: write a `ReactFiberConfig.<renderer>.js`, register the renderer in `scripts/shared/inlinedHostConfigs.js` and add a fork rule, and you get a new React renderer sharing the reconciler unchanged. Bundles are similarly table-driven — add an entry to `scripts/rollup/bundles.js` and a version to `ReactVersions.js` and the build/publish pipeline picks it up. Inside the compiler, the pass list in `Pipeline.ts` / `pipeline.rs` is the ordered registry, `HIR/Globals.ts` is where hook aliasing signatures are declared, and `Environment.ts` is where feature flags live. For tooling, the ESLint plugin merges rules from a `allRules` map, the MCP servers register tools with `server.tool(name, description, schema, handler)`, and Jest behaviour is extended via `@gate` flags declared in `TestFlags.js`.

claims.claim: New renderers plug in through the host-config shim: implement the interface, then register in `scripts/shared/inlinedHostConfigs.js` with a `shortName` and `entryPoints`, and add a substitution branch in `scripts/rollup/forks.js` for `./packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberConfig.js`.

`packages/react-noop-renderer` is the reference implementation of that extension point — a full renderer with `persistent.js`, `server.js`, `flight-client.js`, `flight-server.js` and `flight-modules.js` variants, used as the testbed for reconciler features.

New publishable packages plug into `ReactVersions.js`: the header states 'Packages will not be published unless they are added here', with `stablePackages` for versioned output and `experimentalPackages` for sha-only builds.

New build outputs plug into the `bundles.js` table via `bundleTypes` and `moduleTypes` (`ISOMORPHIC`, `RENDERER`, …); `scripts/rollup/build.js#shouldSkipBundle` then decides per bundle×type whether to emit.

`scripts/rollup/forks.js` is itself an extension registry — a map from module path to a substitution function, currently covering `ReactSharedInternals`, `ReactDOMSharedInternals`, `ReactFeatureFlags`, `SchedulerFeatureFlags`, `DefaultPrepareStackTrace`, `ReactFiberConfig`, `ReactServerStreamConfig`, `ReactFizzConfig`, `ReactFlightServerConfig`, `ReactFlightClientConfig`, `EventListener`, `useSyncExternalStore` and `isServerEnvironment`.

New runtime behaviour is introduced behind a flag in `packages/shared/ReactFeatureFlags.js`, mirrored into every fork under `packages/shared/forks/`, and surfaced to tests automatically as a `@gate` name by `TestFlags.js` (which requires `shared/ReactFeatureFlags` on demand).

The reconciler exposes a stable seam for schedulers: `ReactFiberRootScheduler.js#scheduleCallback` wraps `Scheduler_scheduleCallback(priorityLevel, callback)`, and the Scheduler itself is forked into `SchedulerMock`, `SchedulerNative`, `SchedulerPostTask` variants.

New compiler passes are inserted by editing the ordered pass list in `Entrypoint/Pipeline.ts` (and its Rust twin `entrypoint/pipeline.rs`); `compiler/CLAUDE.md` mandates reading `docs/passes/` for the pass being changed first.

Hook semantics are extensible through aliasing signatures registered in `src/HIR/Globals.ts` via `addHook(DEFAULT_SHAPES, {positionalParams, restParam, returnType, calleeEffect, hookKind, returnValueKind, aliasing: {receiver, params, rest, returns, temporaries, effects}}, id)` — missing an `aliasing` block silently falls back to `DefaultNonmutatingHook`.

Compiler feature flags are configured in `src/HIR/Environment.ts` and can be overridden per test fixture by a first-line comment pragma (e.g. `// enableJsxOutlining @enableNameAnonymousFunctions:false`).

The Rust crates are the extension surface for the port: eleven single-responsibility crates (`react_compiler_lowering`, `_ssa`, `_typeinference`, `_inference`, `_optimization`, `_reactive_scopes`, `_validation`, `_hir`, `_ast`, `_diagnostics`, `_utils`) wired through `Cargo.toml` workspace dependencies.

The ESLint plugin composes its rule table from two hand-written rules plus a spread of `allRules` from `shared/ReactCompiler`, and derives `recommended`/`recommendedLatest` presets by mapping compiler severities through `mapErrorSeverityToESlint` — new compiler diagnostics become lint rules without touching `index.ts`.

MCP tools are registered declaratively: `server.tool(name, description, zodSchema, handler)` in `react-mcp-server/src/index.ts`, with tool implementations kept in `src/tools/` (`runtimePerf`, `componentTree`).

Agent-facing workflows are extensible through `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` — currently `verify`, `test`, `fix`, `flow`, `flags`, `feature-flags` and `extract-errors`, each a self-contained markdown procedure with frontmatter.

Error messages are extended through `scripts/error-codes/codes.json`: new prod error strings are auto-assigned the next integer code by `extract-errors.js`, so adding a user-visible `throw` means running `yarn extract-errors` and committing the JSON delta.

agent_handoff.summary: Treat `/compiler/` and everything else as two separate projects with separate package managers, lockfiles, CI workflows and conventions — the root `CLAUDE.md` says so explicitly, and `compiler/CLAUDE.md` even documents Sapling (`sl`) rather than git for that subtree. Never run `jest` or `rollup` directly; use `yarn test` / `yarn flow` / `yarn linc` / `yarn prettier`, and let CI do builds. The single most important structural fact to internalise before editing is the fork/shim system: `ReactFiberConfig`, `ReactFeatureFlags` and the flight/fizz configs resolve differently under Rollup, Jest and Flow, so 'it works in one channel' is not a signal. Read the work loop, the root scheduler and the feature-flag file before touching reconciler behaviour, and read the relevant `docs/passes/` doc before touching a compiler pass.

claims.claim: The repo is explicitly split: root `CLAUDE.md` scopes itself to 'All files outside `/compiler/`' and defers the compiler to its own instructions; `compiler/` has its own `package.json`, `yarn.lock`, `Cargo.toml` and CI workflows.

Read first, in order: `CLAUDE.md`, `packages/react-dom/src/client/ReactDOMRoot.js` (entry), `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberWorkLoop.js` (the engine), `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberRootScheduler.js` (when work runs), `packages/shared/ReactFeatureFlags.js` (what's on), and `scripts/rollup/forks.js` + `scripts/shared/inlinedHostConfigs.js` (how modules actually resolve).

The prescribed pre-commit gate is `/verify`: `yarn prettier` → `yarn linc` (stop on failure), then `/flow`, `/test` and `/test www` in parallel — mirroring the CI jobs, so passing it locally is a strong predictor of green CI.
Yarn 1 is mandatory (`packageManager: yarn@1.22.22`) and Node is pinned by `.nvmrc`, which every CI job consumes via `node-version-file: '.nvmrc'`.

Do not invoke Jest directly — the root `jest.testRegex` deliberately points at `scripts/jest/dont-run-jest-directly.js`; run `yarn test -r <channel> --env <env>` instead, and `yarn test-www` / `yarn test-stable` for the common channels.

Do not build locally unless told to: root `CLAUDE.md` states 'Builds are handled by CI', and `yarn build` runs a multi-channel Rollup + Closure pipeline that also shells out to git and rewrites versions.
Adding a feature flag is a multi-file edit: the base `packages/shared/ReactFeatureFlags.js` plus each of the 13 forks under `packages/shared/forks/`, verified by `yarn flags` and the CI `flags` job.

Adding a user-visible `throw` requires running `yarn extract-errors` and committing the new entry in `scripts/error-codes/codes.json`; the script greps the `build` directory, so it only works after a build exists.
Tests that depend on a flag or channel must carry a `// @gate <expr>` pragma (supports `&&`, `!`, multiple gates); `FIXME`/`TODO` are reserved gate names that disable a test wholesale.

Compiler work has its own loop: `yarn snap` to run fixtures, `yarn snap -p <pattern> -d` to dump per-pass HIR, `yarn snap -u` to update `.expect.md`, `yarn snap compile <path>` for arbitrary files, `yarn snap minimize <path>` to shrink a repro.

Before implementing from a Rust-port plan doc, `compiler/CLAUDE.md` requires checking `git log --oneline --grep="<plan-name>"` and the plan's Remaining Work section; afterwards update the plan status, run `/compiler-verify`, and ensure `compiler/scripts/test-babel-ast.sh` passes.

Trap: `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberConfig.js` throws on import by design. If a new test or script resolves it, the fix is registering the renderer in `scripts/jest/setupHostConfigs.js` / `inlinedHostConfigs.js`, not editing the shim.

Trap: `packages/react/src/` contains parallel client and server builds of the same package (`ReactClient.js`, `ReactServer.js`, `ReactServer.experimental.js`, `ReactServer.fb.js`, `ReactSharedInternalsClient.js` vs `…Server.js`) — an export added to one is not automatically present in the other.

Safe-to-edit boundaries: `fixtures/` are manual-test apps (only `fixtures/flight` has automated e2e), `scripts/` is developer tooling, and `packages/*/src/__tests__/` are tests. High-caution zones are `ReactFiberWorkLoop.js`, `ReactFiberCommitWork.js`, `ReactFiberHooks.js`, `ReactFizzServer.js`, `ReactFlightServer.js` and anything under `scripts/rollup/` or `scripts/release/`.

Flow is the type system for runtime code (`flow-bin@^0.317.0`, `postinstall` runs `scripts/flow/createFlowConfigs.js` to generate per-renderer configs) while the compiler and ESLint plugin are TypeScript — so `@flow` pragmas and `$FlowFixMe` suppressions are normal in `packages/` and out of place in `compiler/`.
